# dagriculture

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/sims1253/dagriculture/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/sims1253/dagriculture/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![pkgdown](https://github.com/sims1253/dagriculture/actions/workflows/pkgdown.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/sims1253/dagriculture/actions/workflows/pkgdown.yaml)
[![Codecov test coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/sims1253/dagriculture/graph/badge.svg)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/sims1253/dagriculture)
<!-- badges: end -->

dagriculture is an R package for task graphs: directed acyclic graphs whose
nodes are steps of a workflow and whose edges are dependencies between them.
It stores the graph, rejects edits that would make it invalid, and tells you
which nodes nothing in the graph blocks (it calls them eligible) and which are
blocked. It does not run anything.

It is meant for people who write a workflow tool or pipeline runner in R and
want the graph model kept apart from execution.
[bayesgrove](https://github.com/sims1253/bayesgrove) uses it this way: it adds
caching, execution and Bayesian-workflow semantics on top.

A graph is a list with a class attribute. Functions that edit a graph return
a new graph and leave their input unchanged, so keeping an old version means
keeping a variable. The editing functions reject duplicate ids, unknown node
kinds, edges to missing nodes and edges that would create a cycle, each with a
typed error (`dagri_error_*`).

## Installation

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("sims1253/dagriculture")
```

## Example

```{r example}
library(dagriculture)

# The registry lists the kinds of node a graph may hold.
registry <- dagri_registry(
  dagri_kind("data_source"),
  dagri_kind("transform")
)

graph <- dagri_graph(registry) |>
  dagri_add_node("raw_data", "data_source") |>
  dagri_add_node("cleaned_data", "transform") |>
  dagri_add_edge(from = "raw_data", to = "cleaned_data", id = "edge_1")

# A pending gate on the edge blocks everything downstream of it.
graph <- dagri_add_gate(graph, edge_id = "edge_1", id = "review_gate")

graph <- dagri_recompute_state(graph)

dagri_eligible(graph)

dagri_blocked(graph)
```

`dagri_plan()` computes state itself, so you can call it on a graph that was
never passed through `dagri_recompute_state()`. External holds are reasons a
caller gives for keeping a node back, for example a policy check. They change
the plan but not the graph, and they do not change which nodes the graph
itself blocks. Here `raw_data` is held: it stays in `plan$eligible`, because
nothing in the graph blocks it, and also appears in `plan$external_blocked`,
as does `cleaned_data` downstream of it:

```{r plan}
plan <- dagri_plan(
  graph,
  external_holds = list(raw_data = "manual_review")
)

plan$topo_order

plan$eligible

plan$external_blocked

plan$pending_gates
```

Resolving the gate unblocks the downstream node:

```{r resolve}
graph <- dagri_resolve_gate(graph, "review_gate") |>
  dagri_recompute_state()

dagri_eligible(graph)
```

To see what changed between two versions, keep both and compare them:

```{r values}
before <- graph
after <- dagri_add_node(graph, "report", "transform")

dagri_graph_diff(before, after)$added_nodes
```

## Concepts

| Concept | What it is |
|---|---|
| Registry and kind | The node types a graph allows, each with an optional input contract and parameter schema |
| Node | A vertex of one kind, with params, metadata and a structural state (`new`, `ready` or `blocked`) |
| Edge | A dependency between two nodes, with its own id and type |
| Gate | A blocker on an edge, `pending` or `resolved`; nodes downstream of a pending gate are blocked |
| Plan | The targets, their topological order, the eligible and blocked nodes, and the pending gates |

The state is structural only. `dagri_recompute_state()` marks a node
`blocked` when a node upstream is blocked or a pending gate sits on an
incoming edge, and `ready` otherwise. States such as "done" or "failed"
belong to the runtime you build on top.

## Other functions

- Neighbors and reachability: `dagri_upstream()`, `dagri_downstream()`,
  `dagri_ancestors()`, `dagri_descendants()`, `dagri_has_path()`.
- Boundary nodes and order: `dagri_roots()`, `dagri_leaves()`,
  `dagri_terminal()`, `dagri_topo_order()`.
- Comparison: `dagri_graph_diff()` lists added, removed and changed nodes,
  edges and gates, and with `include_values = TRUE` the old and new values.
- Tables: `dagri_nodes_df()`, `dagri_edges_df()` and `dagri_gates_df()` return
  data frames.
- Diagrams: `dagri_mermaid()` returns Mermaid flowchart text.

## Limits

dagriculture does not execute, cache or schedule nodes. Write a runtime for
that, or use one such as bayesgrove.

It handles typed task graphs, not general network analysis. Use igraph for
that.

It does not read or write files. A graph that holds only plain data can be
written as JSON; the
[serialization article](https://sims1253.github.io/dagriculture/articles/serialization-boundary.html) gives a writer and
reader that round-trip a graph.

Every function that takes `metadata` rejects closures, environments,
formulas and other code-bearing values among its elements, at any depth.
`dagri_kind()` requires a `param_schema`, if given, to be a named list with
no functions among its elements, but accepts formulas and environments in
it. Neither check looks at attributes, so a value can still carry code
there. Node `params` are not checked, except that
`dagri_add_node()` requires the names in the kind's input contract. A graph
loaded from an RDS file or edited by hand is checked only for its structure,
its references and self-loops. Longer cycles are found by
`dagri_topo_order()`, `dagri_recompute_state()` and `dagri_plan()`. Nothing
checks it again for
code-bearing values, so load graphs only from sources you trust, or check
them as the [serialization article](https://sims1253.github.io/dagriculture/articles/serialization-boundary.html) shows.
